Abstract
Cyber-physical systems are typically implemented in software as
a set of real-time control tasks. Timing uncertainty at the low-
level scheduling layer can lead to deadline misses of control tasks,
that affects control performance and may violate safety properties
associated with the high-level control applications. We present a
technique to detect and repair control safety violations by synthe-
sizing a scheduler patch – a pre-computed list of jobs to be not
scheduled at runtime – that eliminates these violations without the
need of modifications at the control or task layer. The technique
utilizes a guess–check–repair loop on top of an exact SMT encoding
of control and scheduling behaviours, enabling efficient packing
of multiple control applications on the execution platform while
guaranteeing control safety.
Keywords
repair, synthesis, scheduler patch, control safety, SMT

Introduction
Cyber-physical systems (CPS) such as automotive systems today
have several millions of lines of code deployed on a distributed
architecture of electronic control units (ECUs). With software in-
creasingly used to monitor and control various features of CPS, the
demand to pack more code per ECU is only rising. This poses the
challenge of ensuring timing correctness for the CPS designer: do all
the control applications meet their timing properties, when imple-
mented in software? CPS development typically follows a separation
of concerns approach wherein the high-level control applications
are designed assuming certain timing guarantees from the low-level

uncertainties at the low-level scheduling layer, such as variation
in execution time of task instances, time-triggered activation of
control tasks facing release jitter, or activation of higher-priority
event-triggered tasks to handle interrupt calls, and the like, deadline
misses can occur in unexpected ways in an execution of the tasks.
Thus meeting timing expectations is increasingly challenging.
The schedule synthesis problem asks whether it is possible to
schedule (control) tasks such that deadline misses can be avoided
altogether, and in case not, can some patterns of deadline misses
be factored in during schedule synthesis to guarantee a high-level
goal e.g., control safety. Given that control systems with feedback
mechanisms are generally designed to be robust to delays in sensing
and actuation, several researchers have used this insight to syn-
thesize schedules admitting non-critical deadline misses to satisfy
control safety or stability. However, most works have attempted
to synthesize static schedules of tasks at hand i.e., a lookup table
that dictates the next task to be scheduled. There are limitations of
static scheduling for CPS, such as:
• Inflexibility: lookup table needs to be recomputed when new
tasks are added
• Inefficiency: the computing resource (processor) time is wasted
e.g., when task instances terminate early, or accounting for
jitter
• Difficult/inefficient to synthesize schedules in the presence
of sporadic tasks
Instead, we propose a different form of schedule synthesis: repair
the safety violations by helping the scheduler discriminate between
task instances that are critical to control safety vs. ones that are not
critical to safety. Non-critical task instances are candidates for not
getting scheduled at runtime, freeing up the computing resource
for the more critical ones. In particular, as the physical plant states
evolve with time, different controllers differ in their sensitivity to
deadline misses (aka missed control updates). This is the key to our
approach: modify the existing scheduler to be sensitive to the high-
level goal of control safety.
Thus, when control safety is violated due to timing uncertainty
at the low-level scheduling layer, instead of synthesizing a new
static schedule i.e., changing the scheduling policy, we synthesize
a scheduler patch for the existing scheduling policy. This patch
is a pre-computed list of (non-critical) task instances, that is made
available to the scheduler at system start, and which it consults at
runtime when making a decision on dispatching a task instance

modified as follows: each time the scheduler is invoked to dispatch
a job for execution from its queue, it consults the patch, and if this

Fig.1 illustrates the integration of our synthesized scheduler
patch in a typical CPS design and development flow. The design
and development process is typically layered, starting with the
control applications at hand, followed by a task layer that real-
izes the software implementation of the controllers, followed by
unavoidable timing uncertainties associated with release and/or
network jitter, sporadic triggers such as interrupts, etc, followed by
the RTOS scheduler layer that is configured for a given scheduling
policy. Given the specifications for control applications, tasks, tim-
ing uncertainty and the scheduling policy, our proposed approach
synthesizes a patch offline. The system scheduler code is modified
to accept this patch as input (at system start): the scheduler does
not schedule jobs listed in the patch at runtime. This is in contrast
to online approaches that need to compute a new decision based
on the current system state: our patch-based job-drop approach
does not involve any computation (other than a list lookup), nor is
concerned about timing uncertainties at runtime (these are already
factored in during the offline patch synthesis phase).
It is worth noting that our proposed repair thus requires the
above small change to the real-time OS scheduler, without any
changes to the control applications (viz. recomputing the controller
gains or the discretization timestep), task specification (viz. modify-
ing task parameters), or the scheduling policy (viz. replacing with
a static schedule). In other words, our approach patches the sched-
uler to guarantee control safety without requiring any changes to
the existing CPS design and layers. The two main challenges in
patching the scheduler are:
• modeling and timing analysis of different layers of the CPS
in order to precisely detect high-level safety violations due
to low-level timing uncertainties, and
• an efficient algorithm that searches through the space of
possible repairs.
Towards addressing these challenges, the main contributions
of our work can be summarized as:
• An exact satisfiability-modulo-theory (SMT) encoding of
control and task behaviour, enabling detection of violations
of control safety properties,
• A procedure that employs a guess-check-refine loop on top
of the SMT encoding to soundly repair safety violations,
synthesizing the desired scheduler patch, and
• Prototype tool implementation and case studies demon-
strating the usefulness of our approach.
While our approach is general and can be applied in a variety of
control, task and scheduling models, for a concrete demonstration,
we choose mostly automotive controllers, task sets admitting a
mix of periodic and sporadic tasks, task parameters admitting non-
determinism in task runs, and non-preemptive earliest deadline first
(NP-EDF) as the scheduling policy. We believe this combination
can model realistic CPS, and in particular, our analysis and repair
approach can benefit safety-critical systems that require formal
guarantees of timing correctness. We remark that our guess-check-
refine procedure is not guaranteed to terminate in general – an
inevitability unless some long-standing open problems in the theory
of recurrence sequences [10] are settled.
The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We present a mo-
tivating example in Sec.1.1, give an overview of our approach in
Sec.1.2, and present related work in Sec.1.3. We present our system
model and encoding in Sec.2 and the repair approach with algo-
rithms, theorem and proof in Sec.3. We present two case studies in
Sec.4 and conclude in Sec.5.

1.2
Proposed approach
Figure 3 illustrates our approach for repairing violations of high-
level control safety properties, arising out of low-level timing un-
certainties at the scheduling layer. The encode step accepts as
input a set of (discrete) control system models (plant and con-
troller) 𝐶1, . . . ,𝐶𝑛along with an initial set of states, safety proper-
ties 𝜙1, . . . ,𝜙𝑛, a set of tasks𝑇1, . . . ,𝑇𝑚, a policy for handling missed
control updates, and an analysis horizon 𝐻, and constructs an SMT
encoding of control and scheduling behaviours i.e., trajectories and
task runs up to the horizon, along with safety and loopback con-
straints. The guess map step uses an SMT engine to solve the system
of constraints to find a candidate assignment 𝐹to the drop flags.
If guess fails i.e., the solver reports unsatisfiability of constraints,
we increment the analysis horizon 𝐻by the LCM of task periods,
reconstruct the encoding and repeat. Else, the check safety step

the solver reports unsatisfiability i.e., there is no violation of control
safety and loopback, we report repair success. Flags that were

to be scheduled for execution, irrespective of whether they would
meet their deadline. Note that the patch computation is a one-time,
offline exercise: the scheduler is supplied this list of jobs at system
start i.e., before setting off the tasks for execution.
If the check safety solver call returns a witness i.e., an error
trace, the extract step identifies the sequence of control updates
for the control system that experienced safety violation. This se-
quence corresponds to the sequence of deadline hits and misses
of the corresponding control task. Clearly, some of the jobs that
missed deadline (and subsequently discarded) by the scheduler were
critical to safety. The must step identifies these jobs by systemati-
cally flipping the deadline misses to hits i.e., enabling the (missed)
control updates, and simulating the control system to validate if
this flipping led to control safety. To enable scheduling of these
critical jobs, (possibly non-critical) jobs occupying the processor
and blocking the critical ones should be identified and discarded by
the scheduler i.e., dropped from the scheduler’s ready queue. This
is computed during the identify may step. The refine step uses
the list of may jobs to refine the constraints on subsequent guesses
of the drop map, by constraining at least one of the drop flags of
may jobs to be true i.e., a candidate for not getting scheduled.
If the must step is unable to identify critical jobs, indicating
failure irreparable by flipping deadline miss to hit, we check if
the error trace violated control safety, and if so, terminate the
procedure reporting repair failure. Otherwise, the error trace
violated loopback bounds, indicating divergence of control states,
which necessitates growing the initial set of states to include these
newly observed ones (adjust step), and restart the analysis.
We summarize the approach as follows:
• The proposed repair approach consists of three intertwined
loops: the first loop refines constraints over 𝐹to synthesize
a correct drop set, the second loop adjusts the initial set of
states to achieve loopback or convergence of trajectories,
and the third loop increases the analysis horizon 𝐻.
• Control and loopback safety is established only when the
SMT solver reports an unsat over the formula encoding
error behaviours.
• While the computed drop set is to be used online by the OS
scheduler, the drop set synthesis involving SMT queries is
entirely offline, which we believe is good engineering prac-
tice: the heavyweight verification and synthesis is carried
out as a one-time offline exercise, and the result (job drop
set) is used in a lightweight manner online.
1.3
Related work
The topic of how control performance is impacted due to low-
level timing uncertainties has been extensively studied [5, 6, 8, 9,
11, 13, 16, 18, 20–22, 27]. These works mainly focus on studying
the impact of deadline misses on control stability as the property
of interest. Except in [27] which jointly models scheduling and
control behaviour, most works either assume a deadline miss model
or it has to be provided by the user, which can lead to pessimistic
analysis in the absence of an exact model of the low-level scheduling
behaviour. We avoid pessimism in our analysis by modeling the
full scheduling semantics including the timing non-determinism
arising from factors like jitter and sporadic arrival of task instances.
Approaches to repairing control performance in the presence
of unavoidable deadline miss, which is the topic of focus in this
work, has been studied in [2, 3, 19, 23, 25, 26]. Several works build
upon the paradigm of weakly-hard constraints [1] in both analysis
and repair of control performance in terms of control stability or
safety. Repair may take the form of adjusting task periods [20],
or discarding the scheduling policy and arriving at a new static
schedule guaranteeing control safety [19, 25, 26], or adjusting the
controller [17, 23].
The work in [26], which extends the approach of [25] to synthe-
size static schedules for control tasks with distinct periods to meet
control safety, is closely related to our approach. The authors pro-
pose to readjust task periods i.e., re-design the controllers with new
periods, along with discovering a set of weakly-hard constraints for
each controller, such that an overall static schedule guaranteeing
control safety can be synthesized. However, as observed, all above
approaches require non-trivial changes to the task specification
or control specification, or they discard the scheduling policy to
arrive at a static schedule. Our approach, in contrast, avoids con-
trol safety violations by discarding pre-computed non-critical task
instances so that the processor is available to service more critical
ones. This makes our approach minimally “invasive” i.e., requiring
no modifications to the control systems, tasks or scheduling policy
(except slightly modifying the OS scheduler). Unlike in [25–27] that
checks or guarantees safety over a bounded horizon, our analysis
guarantees both safety and state convergence over infinite control
evolution by checking that states do not diverge at the end of the
job drop window.

the symbolic variables 𝑟,𝑠,𝑒, otherwise the solutions of the SMT
formula can lead to spurious runs.

Experiments
We implemented the algorithms in a prototype tool built using
Python3 scripts and the Z3 SMT solver (version 4.11) via API access.
Most benchmarks were adapted from [24]. All experiments were
run on a laptop running Ubuntu 22 64-bit OS on an Intel i5 processor
with 16GB RAM.

4.3
Comparative evaluation
We present a brief comparison of our tool, named Patcher, with
the tool in [26], which we refer to as StaticSched, though our
approaches and solutions differ: Patcher synthesizes a job drop
list that is to be used at runtime by the scheduler, and StaticSched
synthesizes a static schedule describing the order of execution of
tasks.
For the example systems presented in Sec. 1.1, both tools are able
to achieve control safety, and Patcher solution (nearly) matches the
solution of StaticSched: both synthesize alternating executions
of the two tasks.
For Case Study 1, again Patcher and StaticSched both succeed
in synthesis. StaticSched allows more execution slots to electronic
wedge compared to the other two control tasks, with recomputing
gains required. This is also observed in the case of Patcher, which
drops only 1 instance of electronic wedge system in the drop list.
For Case Study 2, while StaticSched can synthesize a static
schedule for the 3 control systems, there is currently no solution
to accommodate the sporadic task in the static schedule. One way
StaticSched could be extended to handle sporadic tasks is that it
reserves a slot for each sporadic instance. However, this not only
wastes the slot in case the sporadic instance does not arrive, it
may cause non-synthesis for sensitive control systems. This clearly
shows the benefit of using Patcher in situations where the task set
includes more than just control tasks.
5
Conclusion and Future Work
We have proposed an approach to detect and repair high-level con-
trol safety violations, arising from low-level timing uncertainties.
Repairing the violation is based on a novel job dropping scheme,
that augments the scheduler with a pre-computed list of jobs that
are not to be scheduled at runtime, taking advantage of the obser-
vation that control systems differ in their sensitivity to deadline
misses at different points of state evolution. Our approach is sound
and minimally invasive i.e., does not require any changes to the
control or task specification, or the scheduling policy. Our initial
exploration in job-sensitive repair of safety violations via patching
the OS scheduler is encouraging as seen from the experiments, and
enables safe packing of multiple control applications on a shared
computing resource.

Abstract: Cyber-physical systems are typically implemented in software as a set of real-time control tasks. Timing uncertainty at the low- level scheduling layer can lead to deadline misses of control tasks, that affects control performance and may violate safety properties associated with the high-level control applications. We present a technique to detect and repair control safety violations by synthe- sizing a scheduler patch – a pre-computed list of jobs to be not scheduled at runtime – that eliminates these violations without the need of modifications at the control or task layer. The technique utilizes a guess–check–repair loop on top of an exact SMT encoding of control and scheduling behaviours, enabling efficient packing of multiple control applications on the execution platform while guaranteeing control safety.
